props.title: People of the Wind

sections.content: **People of the Wind** (1976) stands as a remarkable ethnographic documentary capturing the epic migration of Iran's Bakhtiari tribes. Following in the tradition of groundbreaking films like Grass: A Nation's Battle for Life (1925), which first documented the Bakhtiari migration, director Anthony Howarth and his team spent months with the nomads during their grueling journey. The film's stunning 16mm cinematography showcases 500 families crossing treacherous mountain passes and raging rivers with 50,000 animals - an ancient tradition that was already beginning to vanish when captured on film.

sections.content: The film represents a vital moment in observational documentary filmmaking, emerging in an era when directors like Frederick Wiseman (**Titicut Follies** (1967)) and the Maysles brothers (**Grey Gardens** (1975)) were pushing the boundaries of direct cinema. **People of the Wind** distinguishes itself through its patient observation of both the grand spectacle of mass migration and intimate family moments, accompanied by Anthony Howarth's thoughtful narration that contextualizes without overshadowing the visual story.

Beyond its ethnographic significance, **People of the Wind** shares DNA with other landmark documentaries about vanishing ways of life, like Robert Flaherty's Nanook of the North (1922) and **Man of Aran** (1934). The film earned an Academy Award nomination for Best Documentary Feature, highlighting Hollywood's growing recognition of observational documentary as a powerful artistic medium. sections.content: The film's influence extends into contemporary works documenting nomadic peoples and traditional lifestyles, such as **The Story of the Weeping Camel** (2003) and **The Eagle Huntress** (2016). Modern filmmakers continue to grapple with similar themes of tradition versus modernity, though few achieve the intimate access and comprehensive scope of Howarth's work with the Bakhtiari.
